title: The 5 Longest-Burning Fires on Earth, Ranked (#1 Predates the Pyramids)

scenes.text: Five fires that never went out, ranked. Number one was burning before the pyramids were built.

scenes.label: Darvaza · 55 years
scenes.text: Number five: the Darvaza gas crater in Turkmenistan. Seventy metres wide, burning since 1971. Around fifty-five years, and finally fading.

scenes.label: Centralia · 64 years
scenes.text: Number four: Centralia, Pennsylvania. A coal-mine fire since 1962. The town had a thousand people in 1980. Now about five.

scenes.label: Jharia · 110 years
scenes.text: Number three: Jharia coalfield, India. Burning since 1916. Over a century, with whole neighbourhoods built on top of it.

scenes.label: Brennender Berg · 350+ years
scenes.text: Number two: the Burning Mountain of Saarland, Germany. Smouldering since the 1600s. Goethe felt the heat through his shoes in 1770.

scenes.label: Burning Mountain · 6,000 years
scenes.text: Number one: Burning Mountain, Australia. A coal seam burning for about six thousand years, creeping south one metre a year.

description:
The five longest-burning fires on Earth, ranked by how long they have been burning.
Burning Mountain (Mount Wingen) in New South Wales is a natural coal-seam fire estimated at 5,500 to 6,000 years old, moving south about a metre a year 30 metres underground. Germany's Brennender Berg has smouldered since about 1668; Jharia's mine fires were first recorded in 1916; Centralia's began in May 1962; the Darvaza crater has burned since 1971 and is now being extinguished.
Which of these would you want to see in person?
first_comment: Canada's Smoking Hills have been burning for centuries too, but nobody knows when they started, so they stay off the list. Which would you put at number one, and what should we rank next?
